title: Problem Solving on Permutation and Combination

lines:
Let's recall the problem in the previous lesson. How many three-letter combinations can be formed from the word MATH? 
Recall that this was represented in combination notation as C(4,3) and there were 4 possible combinations. However, in permutation, there were 24 possible arrangements. Those arrangements are shown below. Notice that the set of the different combinations formed is the subset of the set of permutations. Each combination of three letters determine 3! = 6 permutations of the letters in the combination:
Table of Combinations and Permutations of 3 letters from the word MATH

Hence, the number of combinations multiplied by 3! gives the number of permutations: C(4,3) • 3! = P(4,3) , or equivalently,  
C(4,3) = \frac{P(4,3)}{3!}

Why do we need to divide it by 3!? This is to count the arrangements of the same group as one since they are already counted in P(4,3). 
Solving for C(n, r), gives you C(n,r) = \frac{P(n,r)}{r!}.
Knowing that P(n,r) = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!}, substitute this in the above equation and in so doing
we get C(n,r) = \frac{\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}}{(n-r)!} Multiplying numerator n!/(n-r)! by the reciprocal of the
